parties: Defendant: Golden Jet Freight Forwarders Limited

facts.F1: On 31st August, 1977, Golden Jet Freight Forwarders Limited secured an aircraft Charter Agreement from Transmeridian Air Cargo Limited for the carriage of cargo.
facts.F2: The aircraft managed by Transmeridian Air Cargo Limited crashed on take-off at Kai Tak in September 1977.
facts.F3: Golden Jet raised five claims against Transmeridian: (1) Charter-hire U.S. $39,842.46, (2) Loss of cargo from Drama K. Co. $97,870.46, (3) Loss of cargo from Tricoville (HK) Limited $36,383.00, (4) Miscellaneous shipment claims from July to September 1978 $39,840.90, and (5) Claim on the abandonment or off-loading of 36 cartons of goods in September 1978 $95,000.
facts.F4: Transmeridian commenced an action against Golden Jet for the charter hire accrued from March to June 1979 in the sum of U.S.$78,123.05.
facts.F5: Golden Jet and Speedway Air Cargo Forwarders Limited commenced an action against Transmeridian in Hong Kong and later in the English Commercial Court, which was held in abeyance and not further prosecuted due to the appointment of receivers and a creditors' voluntary winding up.
facts.F6: The period of limitation for raising claims on the first three heads of Golden Jet's claim expired on the 1st September, 1979.
facts.F7: The court distinguished between legal set-off, counterclaim, and equitable set-off, and applied these principles to Golden Jet's claim.
facts.F8: Section 35 of the Limitation Ordinance was applied to determine the effect on set-off and counterclaim.
facts.F9: The court considered the characteristics of voyage charters and time charters to distinguish between freight and hire.
facts.F10: The difference between freight in a voyage charter and hire in a time charter was considered to determine the applicability of the strict rule against deduction, abatement, or recoupment.

lawsuit_type: Appeal from Master's Decision and application by summons for consolidation with another action
reference_issues: Whether Golden Jet can raise a legal set-off against Transmeridian's claim for charter hire.
Whether the strict rule against deduction, abatement, or recoupment from freight applies to a claim for air charter hire.

facts.F2: Kam used to be one of two tenants-in-common in equal shares of the property located at the Remaining Portion of Kowloon Inland Lot No 1102.
facts.F3: The Property was resumed by the Government on 3 April 1997 pursuant to the terms of the Lands Resumption Ordinance.
facts.F4: On 30 April 1997, a letter was issued by the Intended Garnishee to Kam and the other tenant-in-common, making an offer of compensation in respect of the resumption of the Property.
facts.F5: The offered amount was HK$16,550,000, with Kam's half share being HK$8,275,000.
facts.F6: The offer lapsed on 29 May 1997 as no written acceptance was received from Kam.
facts.F7: On 6 June 1997, another letter was issued by the Intended Garnishee to Kam and the other tenant-in-common, offering a provisional payment in the sum of HK$14,895,000.
facts.F8: Kam accepted his share of the provisional payment in the sum of HK$7,447,500 on 11 June 1997.
facts.F9: No claim in respect of the resumption of the Property has ever been submitted by Kam or the Government to the Lands Tribunal.
facts.F10: The plaintiff took out the summonses on 1 November 2017, which were subsequently dismissed by Master Lo on 14 March 2018.
facts.F11: The plaintiff filed his Notices of Appeal on 25 and 30 April 2018, seeking to enforce the costs orders against the defendant.
facts.F12: The Chief Justice emphasized the importance of adopting a purposive approach to statutory construction in Yung Chi Keung v Protection of Wages on Insolvency Board.

requested_remedy: charter hire accrued from March to June 1979 in the sum of U.S.$78,123.05 with costs
parties: Defendant: Golden Jet Freight Forwarders Limited

facts.F1: Transmeridian Air Cargo Limited managed an aircraft that crashed on take-off at Kai Tak in September 1977.
facts.F2: Golden Jet Freight Forwarders Limited had secured an aircraft Charter Agreement from Transmeridian for the carriage of cargo.
facts.F3: As a result of the crash, five claims arose against Transmeridian, but Golden Jet raised all these five claims before Transmeridian's Hong Kong action commenced in February 1980.
facts.F4: On 13th August 1979, Golden Jet commenced an action in Hong Kong High Court Action No.3488 of 1979, which included the five claims of Golden Jet against Transmeridian and its associate company, the Transmeridian Air Cargo (HK) Limited.
facts.F5: On 14th August 1979, Golden Jet intimated to Transmeridian that the charter hire due from Golden Jet and Speedway Air Cargo Forwarders Limited would be set off.
facts.F6: A similar action was commenced by Golden Jet and Speedway Air Cargo Forwarders Limited against Transmeridian and Transmeridian (HK) in the English Commercial Court, which was later held in abeyance by consent.
facts.F7: In March 1980, receivers were appointed in Transmeridian under a Debenture, and in October 1980, there was a creditors' voluntary winding up, causing the English action to not proceed further.
facts.F8: On 23rd February 1980, Transmeridian commenced its present Hong Kong Action 914 against Golden Jet for the said charter hire accrued from March to June 1979.
facts.F9: In May 1980, an Order 14 summons was taken out, and on the 21st January, 1982 the Master granted Transmeridian leave to sign final judgment against Golden Jet in the sum of U.S.$78,123.05 with costs.
facts.F10: Golden Jet appealed against that decision of the Master, arguing that they have a bona fide triable defence.
facts.F11: Lord Denning M.R. explained the difference between a counterclaim, a legal set-off and an equitable set-off in Henriksens Rederi v. Rolimpex (The Brede).
facts.F12: Lord Wilberforce observed in Aries Tanker Corporation v. Total Transport Ltd. that there is no case of the strict rule against deduction from freight having been extended to contracts of any kind of carriage.
facts.F13: The rules against deduction, abatement, or recoupment from freight applied in English law for over a century.
facts.F14: In marine cases under English Law, the strict rule only applied to voyage charters.

lawsuit_type: High Court Action, Defendant's Appeal from Master's Decision and Order 14 summons for consolidation with another action
reference_issues: Whether Golden Jet can raise a legal set-off against Transmeridian.
Whether the strict rule against deduction, abatement, or recoupment from freight should be extended beyond the case of a voyage charter.

facts.F1: The plaintiff and CCL Systems Ltd (CCL) entered into a facility letter dated 9 June 1993 (the 1993 Facility Letter), which extended banking facilities to CCL, including an overdraft, an import line, and a corporate credit card.
facts.F2: The 1993 Facility Letter required a new joint and several guarantee from the directors of CCL, including the defendant, for a maximum liability of HK$6,000,000.
facts.F3: The defendant signed the guarantee on 10 June 1993 (the Guarantee).
facts.F4: The defendant resigned as a director of CCL in April 1998 and requested to be released as a guarantor under the Guarantee.
facts.F5: The plaintiff took steps to renew and revise the facilities extended to CCL by a facility letter dated 16 June 1999 (the 1999 Facility Letter) without the defendant's knowledge or consent.
facts.F6: The 1999 Facility Letter introduced a new loan facility of HK$2,000,000.
facts.F7: The defendant protested the renewal of the facilities without his consent and claimed that he was no longer bound by the Guarantee.
facts.F8: The plaintiff withdrew the banking facilities and cancelled the credit limits by a letter dated 4 November 1999 (the Withdrawal Letter).
facts.F9: The plaintiff subsequently consolidated CSL's outstanding loans and advances by a letter dated 25 July 2000 (the 2000 Facility Letter).
facts.F10: CSL went into compulsory liquidation by an order dated 26 February 2001.
facts.F11: The plaintiff commenced the present proceedings against the defendant, claiming the sum of HK$2,265,661.71 with interest.
facts.F12: The rule in Holme v. Brunskill provides that any variation of the underlying contract that is not manifestly insubstantial or incapable of prejudicing the surety will discharge the surety from his obligations under the contract of guarantee.
facts.F13: The definition of 'Banking Facilities' and 'Guaranteed Moneys' in the Guarantee provides that the extent of the obligations under the Guarantee arose specifically out of the 1993 Facility Letter and any subsequent renewal with the defendant's knowledge and consent.
facts.F14: The court found that the extension of the loan facility in the 1999 Facility Letter was a material variation of the original contract and that the defendant was thereby discharged.
facts.F15: Clause 9 of the Guarantee did not exclude the operation of the rule in Holme v. Brunskill.
facts.F16: The language of Clause 9 of the Guarantee was not specific enough to include the giving of time by virtue of the 2000 Facility Letter.

facts.F4: The defendant’s application is based on the ground that it has a strong appeal or that there is a strong likelihood that its appeal would succeed.
facts.F5: The principal point in the defendant’s appeal is the finding that when the defendant issued the letter of termination dated 23 April 2008, it was not entitled to treat the Subcontract as having been repudiated by the plaintiff.
facts.F6: The defendant complains there was a failure to adhere to the principle in Creatiles Building Materials Co Ltd v. To’s Universe Construction Ltd [2003] 2 HKLRD 309 at para.23 in deciding whether the plaintiff had evinced an intention not to be bound by the Subcontract.
facts.F7: The court had taken into consideration a number of matters, including the late payments and under payments and the conduct of the parties after the completion of the work on T1 to T6 in coming to the finding complained of.
facts.F8: The relevant conduct of the parties in the period after the Chinese New Year in 2008 until the defendant’s letter of termination include: engaging in discussions with a view to settling the accounts, reaching consensus on a number of the disputes, the making of further payments based upon the consensus reached, agreeing that the defendant would proceed with the work of the remaining six towers pending further discussions on the outstanding differences on the accounts for T1 to T6, and simultaneously engaging in discussions on and making preparations for the work for the remaining six towers.
facts.F9: It is the defendant’s case and also the evidence of its witnesses that what triggered the letter of termination was the fact that the 9th payment had not included the 1% discount rebate.
facts.F10: The Subcontract is a re-measurement contract such that there are bound to be differences between the amount of payment applied for and the amount of the payments made.
facts.F11: A hearing of a stay of execution application is not the occasion to embark upon a detailed examination of the merits of the appeal.
facts.F12: The relevant conduct of the parties in the period after the Chinese New Year in 2008 until the defendant’s letter of termination is relevant to the determination of the appeal.

lawsuit_type: Application for stay of execution of judgment pending appeal
reference_issues: Whether the defendant has demonstrated that the strength of its appeal is such as to support a stay of execution.

claim: The applicants applied to set aside the respective statutory demands on the ground that the alleged debt in each statutory demand is disputed on substantial grounds.
requested_remedy: The applicants applied to set aside the respective statutory demands on the ground that the alleged debt in each statutory demand is disputed on substantial grounds.
parties: Plaintiff: Lio Weng Tong and Ma Song Qiondy

facts.F1: Koofy Development Limited ('Koofy') entered into an Exclusive Distributor Agreement with Athena Solutions Pty Ltd ('Athena') for worldwide distribution of Koofy’s goods.
facts.F2: Koofy and the respondent entered into a trade financing agreement, where Koofy assigned accounts receivables from Athena to the respondent, and the respondent would pay Koofy a percentage of the face value of these receivables upfront.
facts.F3: The two applicants are the shareholders and directors of Koofy.
facts.F4: The respondent engages in the business of trade financing.
facts.F5: A Deed of Assignment was executed, and due notice of assignment was given to Athena.
facts.F6: Athena defaulted on a payment, and the respondent never received any payment from Athena.
facts.F7: Athena raised a dispute regarding the payment, and the respondent determined, under the agreement's Clause 8 Proviso, that the non-payment by Athena was for reasons other than Athena's financial inability.
facts.F8: Pursuant to this conversion, Koofy became obliged to pay the various sums set out in the statutory demands to the respondent.
facts.F9: Since Koofy defaulted, the two applicants, being the guarantors, are indebted to the respondent for those sums.
facts.F10: The dispute raised by Athena is of no merit.
facts.F11: There is a dispute on what were the finalized terms of agreement between Koofy and Athena.
facts.F12: There is absolutely no evidence of any financial inability on the part of Athena.

lawsuit_type: Application to set aside a statutory demand
reference_issues: Whether it can be argued that the respondent acted unreasonably in not concluding that the non-payment by Athena was due to their financial inability.

claim: The plaintiffs seek an injunction to restrain the Bank from presenting any petition for the winding up of the Applicants based on the amounts claimed in 3 statutory demands dated 3 May 2000 totalling HK$9,080,792.62. The plaintiffs also apply to set aside the statutory demands dated 1 May 2000 served on each of the Individual Applicants.
requested_remedy: The plaintiffs seek an injunction to restrain the Bank from presenting any petition for the winding up of the Applicants based on the amounts claimed in 3 statutory demands dated 3 May 2000 totalling HK$9,080,792.62. The plaintiffs also apply to set aside the statutory demands dated 1 May 2000 served on each of the Individual Applicants.
parties: Plaintiff: The World Enterprises (Holdings) Limited, China Fleet Limited, Expert Bright Investments Limited, Chan Siu Lam, Wada Junji, Leung Chi Kong, Siu Chi Fung Peter, Law Wai Kwong, Siu Chi Lim Steve
Defendant: The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation Limited

facts.F1: The Applicants are companies in the same group, and the 1st Applicant, The World Enterprises (Holdings) Limited, is the holding company of the group.
facts.F2: The 2nd Applicant and the 3rd Applicant are property holding companies, and they are customers of the Respondent, the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation Limited.
facts.F3: The Applicants seek an injunction to restrain the Bank from presenting any petition for the winding up of the Applicants based on the amounts claimed in 3 statutory demands dated 3 May 2000 totalling HK$9,080,792.62.
facts.F4: Various properties were mortgaged by the Companies to the Bank between July 1988 and September 1997, and guarantees were given by the Individual Applicants during this period when facilities were extended by the Bank.
facts.F5: Following re-structuring negotiations with the Bank in 1999 and in order to reduce their liabilities towards the Bank, the Companies delivered up vacant possession of the aforesaid properties to the Bank for sale.
facts.F6: On 25 May 2000, directions were given for the two applications to be heard together as the same evidence would be relied on by the Companies and the Individual Applicants in their applications.
facts.F7: The Bank gave an undertaking not to present any petition based on the statutory demands before the adjourned hearing and an early date was given for the adjourned hearing.
facts.F8: Units 5-9 were sold by the Bank for HK$21.4 million, and Units 2-4 were sold for HK$14.1 million.
facts.F9: The Companies had obtained a valuation from CB Richard Ellis dated 17 March 2000, which gave an open market value of Units 5-9 as at 11 October 1999 on a break-up basis at HK$27.8 million, and Units 2-4 at HK$16 million.
facts.F10: The difference between the actual selling prices and the valuations of Richard Ellis for Units 5-9 and Units 2-4 would be HK$8.3 million in the aggregate.
facts.F11: The Applicants established substantial grounds for their claim against the Bank in respect of the sale of Units 5-9 and Units 2-4.
facts.F12: The Applicants demonstrated on sufficiently credible evidence that they have a claim against the Bank for acting in breach of its duty as a mortgagee in the sale of Units 5-9 on substantial grounds.
facts.F13: The Applicants established substantial grounds for a claim which may equal or exceed the total indebtedness in the statutory demand.

lawsuit_type: Applications by way of a Notice of Originating Motion (HCMP No. 2468 of 2000) and notices of motion (HCSD Nos 17-22 of 2000)
reference_issues: Whether the Bank has a duty to take reasonable care to obtain a proper price or the true market value for the mortgaged property at the time of sale.
Whether the Applicants have a substantial counterclaim which equals or exceeds the amount of the debt claimed in the statutory demands.

claim: The plaintiff complains that the capitalisation of the Pioneer loans would be prejudicial to the independent shareholders of the 7th defendant because it is said the 2nd defendant was connected to the 1st defendant and the 1st defendant was a connected person with the 7th defendant. It is said that the loans were ultra vires and illegal.
requested_remedy: The plaintiff complains that the capitalisation of the Pioneer loans would be prejudicial to the independent shareholders of the 7th defendant because it is said the 2nd defendant was connected to the 1st defendant and the 1st defendant was a connected person with the 7th defendant. It is said that the loans were ultra vires and illegal.

facts.F1: The writ of summons with a statement of claim endorsed was issued in this case on 16 December 2015.
facts.F2: The plaintiff alleges that there was an illicit scheme operated by the 1st defendant to channel funds wrongfully obtained to the 7th defendant which is a listed company in Hong Kong.
facts.F3: The 1st defendant procured the 4th, 5th and 6th defendants, which are all listed companies in Korea, to lend money to the 3rd defendant, a Korean company said to be 51% owned by the 4th defendant.
facts.F4: The 3rd defendant would then inject the money into its own wholly owned subsidiary, the 2nd defendant.
facts.F5: The 2nd defendant would then lend the money to the 7th defendant, and these loans to the 7th defendant, called “Pioneer loans,” were a money laundering activity and harmful to the 4th, 5th and 6th defendants.
facts.F6: On 1 December 2015, the 7th defendant entered into certain loan capitalisation agreements with a number of its creditors, including the 2nd defendant.
facts.F7: Under the agreement with the 2nd defendant, the 7th defendant would issue a maximum of 162,505,317 new shares to the 2nd defendant to capitalise the Pioneer loans.
facts.F8: The relevant public announcement, which is dated 1 December 2015, made clear that the completion of the loan capitalisation exercise would be subject to shareholders’ approval, and in respect of certain creditors, subject to approval by independent shareholders, at an extraordinary general meeting of the 7th defendant to be held.
facts.F9: The original long-stop date for the capitalisation exercise was 29 February 2016, but it has since been extended to August 2016.
facts.F10: The plaintiff issued a summons pursuant to Order 14 of the Rules of the High Court for summary judgment against the 2nd defendant that the 2nd defendant should forfeit all of its loans made to the 7th defendant on 14 March 2016.
facts.F11: The plaintiff issued the summons seeking an injunction order for the 2nd defendant be restrained from taking any steps to sell, in any direct or indirect manner, alter the form of its “Pioneer Loans,” and continue to be involved or engaged in any discussions or agreements with any party about possible transaction relating to its Pioneer Loans, until the Summary Judgment has been made by the Court on 15 March 2016.
facts.F12: There is an indictment against the 1st defendant in Korea, which is yet to be tried and proved.
facts.F13: The court does not consider the 1st defendant's indictment from Korea as solid evidence.
facts.F14: The loan capitalisation exercise would be subject to advice from independent financial advisors and would be subject to shareholders’ approval at the EGM to be held and to the approval of the Listing Committee of the Stock Exchange in granting listing of and permission to deal in the capitalisation shares.

lawsuit_type: Interlocutory injunction application
reference_issues: Whether the plaintiff has a legitimate interest in seeking an injunction to restrain the 2nd defendant from dealing with its own private property.
Whether the capitalisation exercise is illegal and ultra vires due to alleged money laundering activities.

claim: Claims for arrears of wages and wages in lieu of notice
requested_remedy: Claims for arrears of wages and wages in lieu of notice
parties: Plaintiff: TSE PAK KAN alias Peter TSE, LAU CHE KEUNG, HON WAI KWONG, LAU SAU LUEN alias Rosline LAU, HO CHO YUEN, FUNG WAI KEI, FRANCIS CHEN, LEE CHI CHEONG TELAN, HSU BOBBY, YAU KWOK KEUNG, POON KIN SANG, IU KONG IM, TSUI YEE WAH BRUMA, LI PAK MOON, TUNG SIK HUNG, FONG YUN FAT, CHEUNG CHEUNG HIN, LEE KA WOO, LAU CHI WING, CHAN SHAN HING BOTTY, LEUNG KIN YIP alias LEUNG CHUN
Defendant: AMOR LIVE HOLDINGS LTD. and AMOR COFFEE HOUSE LTD.

facts.F1: The appellants, Amor Live Holdings Ltd. and Amor Coffee House Ltd., were the lessees of the 1st and 2nd floors of the Magnolia Building in Tin Hau Temple Road.
facts.F2: The appellants permitted the 1st and 2nd defendants to run the nightclub on the 2nd floor, which was thereafter renamed 'Lounge de Scorpio'.
facts.F3: The agreement between the parties was labelled as a 'Service Agreement' and contained provisions typical of an employment contract.
facts.F4: The 1st and 2nd defendants paid a post-dated cheque for the first month's guaranteed profits, which was dishonoured on its presentation for payment.
facts.F5: The nightclub was locked up by the appellants and ceased to carry on business.
facts.F6: 21 claimants, who were employees of the nightclub, filed claims against the appellants for arrears of wages and wages in lieu of notice.
facts.F7: The Labour Tribunal found in favour of the claimants, and the appellants appealed against the decision.
facts.F8: The appellants argued that the claimants were not their employees, but rather sub-servants of the 1st and 2nd defendants, who operated the nightclub independently.
facts.F9: The Court of Appeal found that the agreement between the parties was a service agreement, and the 1st and 2nd defendants were employees of the appellants.
facts.F10: The Court also found that the 1st and 2nd defendants were authorized to engage staff on behalf of the appellants, and the successful claimants were employees of the appellants.
facts.F11: The appellants acted consistently with the relationship of employer and employee with respect to the claimants.
facts.F12: The 1st and 2nd defendants complied with the contractual provisions of the service agreement.

lawsuit_type: Labour Tribunal Appeal
reference_issues: Whether the claimants were employees of the appellants or sub-servants of the 1st and 2nd defendants.
Whether the 1st and 2nd defendants were authorized to engage staff on behalf of the appellants.

Challinor v. Taylor [1971] The Times, December 22 (N.I.R.C.)

Chitty on Contract Vol. 2, 24th Ed. G 3508, 3514

claim: The Plaintiffs claimed for summary judgment against the Defendant in the amount of $580,000 and to strike out the counterclaim filed by the Defendant.

facts.F1: The Defendant entered into a service agreement with the 1st Plaintiff to serve as the chief executive officer of a newspaper, 'The Observer Star', operated by the Plaintiffs' group for a term of 3 years commencing on 1 June 2004.
facts.F2: The Defendant would receive a monthly service fee of $70,000 under the Service Agreement.
facts.F3: The service fee for the first 12 months, in the sum of $840,000, was paid by the 2nd Plaintiff upon the signing of the Service Agreement.
facts.F4: The advance payment would be used to set-off against the subsequent 36 months of service fee payable to the Defendant under the Service Agreement.
facts.F5: Either party would have the right to terminate the Service Agreement by giving six months' written notice of termination.
facts.F6: The Defendant served a resignation notice on the 1st Plaintiff to terminate the Service Agreement on 3 February 2005.
facts.F7: The parties signed a supplemental agreement dated 8 October 2005 ('the Supplemental Agreement'), whereby it was agreed that if the Defendant could generate advertising income totalling $1.2 million for the two newspapers, 'Community Star' and the Newspaper, operated by the Plaintiffs' group between September and November 2004, the Defendant would not be liable to repay the Plaintiffs the outstanding advance service fee.
facts.F8: The Defendant failed to meet the set target for advertising income.
facts.F9: An agreement dated 28 December 2004 ('the December Agreement') was made between both Plaintiffs and the Defendant, which provided for an early termination of the Service Agreement and the Supplemental Agreement on 30 November 2004, and the Defendant had to return the sum of $580,000 to the 2nd Plaintiff by 10 instalments.
facts.F10: If the Defendant failed to make any of the instalment payments, the 2nd Plaintiff should be entitled to recover from the Defendant the whole amount of the outstanding balance.
facts.F11: The Defendant handed 10 cheques to the Plaintiffs as security for the repayments.
facts.F12: There were discussions between the parties prior to the December Agreement.

lawsuit_type: Summary judgment application
reference_issues: Whether the Defendant's defences are arguable
Whether the December Agreement is a valid settlement agreement between the parties

claim: declarations that the shares and proceeds are his, an order that the defendant transfer and pay them over, interest on the sum of $2,376,315, and a return of the unbanked cheque
requested_remedy: declarations that the shares and proceeds are his, an order that the defendant transfer and pay them over, interest on the sum of $2,376,315, and a return of the unbanked cheque

facts.F1: The defendant is a licensed stockbroker in Hong Kong.
facts.F2: A prospective new client introduced himself to an officer of the defendant as Chung Kwok Wing and produced an identity card and a Bank of China credit card statement.
facts.F3: In fact, the man concerned was a fraudster who had used a stolen identity card.
facts.F4: An account was opened for Chung and he deposited by cheque the sum of $3,400,000 to purchase shares.
facts.F5: The plaintiff agreed to sell 32 million shares in Dransfield Holdings Limited to Chung at $0.125 each for a total of $4 million.
facts.F6: The defendant recorded the transaction into the Stock Exchange Trading System and reserved the right to reject it before the market opened the following day.
facts.F7: The plaintiff offered to guarantee Chung’s performance by covering his cheque and depositing the balance of the $4 million.
facts.F8: The defendant sold a total of 21,488,000 shares at Chung’s instruction, netting $2,041,215.
facts.F9: Chung’s cheque bounced and subsequent inquiry revealed it had been drawn on an account already closed.
facts.F10: The defendant froze Chung's account pending the outcome of the investigation and the plaintiff sought a return of the undisposed of shares and the balance of funds.
facts.F11: The plaintiff issued a writ and a statement of claim, alleging that the shares and proceeds constituted the unjust enrichment of Chung, which the defendant held upon constructive trust for the plaintiff.
facts.F12: Chung was a crook and had disappeared.
facts.F13: The defendant had recovered the cost of the shares and commissions on purchase and sale.
facts.F14: The plaintiff became the victim of the fraud perpetrated by Chung.

lawsuit_type: appeal by rehearing from a Master’s decision
reference_issues: Whether the defendant holds the shares in trust for the plaintiff, and must return them.
Whether the plaintiff is entitled to interest on the sum of $2,376,315 and a return of the unbanked cheque.

claim: the sum of HK$6,612,954.40 with interest and costs
requested_remedy: the sum of HK$6,612,954.40 with interest and costs
parties: Defendant: Cineaste International Ltd and Wong Kwong Biu

facts.F1: The 1st defendant, Cineaste International Ltd, engaged the plaintiff as its printer for a computer magazine in 1997, and Mr Wong, the senior sales manager, dealt with the 2nd defendant in all essential matters in the business relationship.
facts.F2: The 2nd defendant was asked to provide a personal guarantee of all the printing costs invoiced by the plaintiff to the 1st defendant in 1997. Similar letters of guarantee were given by the 2nd defendant to the plaintiff in 1999 and 2000.
facts.F3: In the second half of 2000, the 1st defendant began to have serious difficulty in meeting payment of the printing charges of the plaintiff, resulting in a meeting between the 2nd defendant, the plaintiff's managing director James Lee Tak Wing, and Mr Wong in July 2000.
facts.F4: The 1st defendant issued 6 post-dated personal cheques for the total sum of HK$3,052,224.40 to pay part of the debt owed by the 1st defendant and its associated company. The cheques were not presented for payment as the 2nd defendant had notified the plaintiff of his difficulties in obtaining funds.
facts.F5: On 2 April 2001, a deed ('the 1st Deed') was made between the plaintiff and the 2nd defendant in which the 2nd defendant agreed and undertook to pay to the plaintiff HK$3,052,224.40, being part of the indebtedness of the 1st defendant and its associated company, by 6 instalments on stipulated dates.
facts.F6: The 2nd defendant met the 1st and 2nd instalment payments in the total sum of HK$1,000,000.00 under the 1st Deed, but no other payment was made.
facts.F7: The 2nd Deed was entered into by the plaintiff, the 1st defendant, and the 2nd defendant on 27 August 2001, with a revised payment schedule, after the 1st defendant's debt had grown to HK$6,712,954.40 by July 2001.
facts.F8: The plaintiff returned to the 2nd defendant the personal cheques of the 2nd defendant that were not presented for payment and given to the plaintiff pursuant to the 1st Deed, and the 2nd defendant issued a new set of personal cheques.
facts.F9: The 1st cheque in the sum of HK$500,000.00 was due for payment on 31 August 2001, but was replaced by 2 cheques dated 1 September 2001 and 5 September 2001 in the respective sums of HK$100,000.00 and HK$400,000.00. The cheque for HK$100,000.00 was paid, but the other cheque was dishonoured when presented for payment on 5 September 2001, resulting in the plaintiff issuing the writ on 15 September 2001.
facts.F10: The plaintiff had incurred expenses for engaging a solicitor to prepare the 1st Deed and the 2nd Deed.
facts.F11: The relationship between Mr Wong and the 2nd defendant did not involve the 2nd defendant placing trust and confidence in Mr Wong or Mr Wong acquiring an ascendancy or domination over the 2nd defendant.

lawsuit_type: appeal from a summary judgment
reference_issues: Whether the 2nd defendant has raised a triable issue on misrepresentation
Whether the 2nd defendant has raised a triable issue on undue influence
